title: Why It's Getting Harder for Some American Women to Find a Husband
summary: Have you ever thought about dating like a game of musical chairs? A new study says that's kind of what's happening with marriage in America right now. And it all starts with a funny story about a musician named Jack Antonoff. Jack went to a high school where most kids were artsy, and he says he was one of the only straight guys there. He joked that the math worked in his favor—he ended up dating actress Scarlett Johansson! That's a silly example, but it shows how having more of one group can change things. Now, let's look at the big picture. In the U.S., women are now more likely to go to college than men. In fact, female students make up almost 60% of college students. Meanwhile, many men without college degrees are struggling with jobs, money, and other problems. So, what does this mean for marriage? The study found that college-educated women are still getting married, but they're often marrying men who didn't go to college—as long as those men earn good money. That leaves women without college degrees with fewer men who have stable jobs to marry. Their marriage rates have dropped a lot, and many are raising kids on their own. It's like the chairs in musical chairs are being taken away. This isn't about love or chemistry—people marry for all kinds of reasons. But when the numbers shift, it can change who ends up together. And that can affect families and even the whole country.
why_it_matters: This shows how your education and the jobs available can affect not just you, but also your future family and relationships.

background_read: Musical chairs is a party game where players walk around chairs and must quickly sit when the music stops. There are fewer chairs than players, so someone is left out.
In the past, more men than women went to college, but that has reversed in recent decades.
Jack Antonoff is a musician and songwriter, and he once dated Scarlett Johansson (an actress famous for playing Black Widow in Marvel movies).
Article_Structure: WHO: American women (especially those with and without college degrees), men without degrees, and researchers.
WHAT: A study finds marriage rates are changing because more women go to college and many men without degrees struggle, making the situation like a game of musical chairs.
WHY: Women are now 60% of college students, and men without degrees have fewer stable jobs, so women without degrees have fewer marriage options.

perspectives.description: College-educated women still get married, and more women in college shows big steps forward for gender equality.
Women without degrees face lower marriage rates and often raise kids alone, which can make family life and money much harder.
Marriage trends always shift with the economy. This is just another numbers game, not about who people love.
